1.0.0.en: Covered him: wrapped him with coverings.

1.0.1.en: David's life was drawing to its close, and he was in his late sixties, for he became king at the age of thirty and died at the age of seventy, that is, he reigned forty years (2 Sam 5:4, 5). He fell ill at the end of his life and could no longer bear the cold of the air; however many heavy garments they put on him and however many coverings they laid over him, he kept feeling cold and shivering. This shows how great David's bodily weakness was and how early his old age had come, which made him unable to manage the kingdom. This encouraged his son Adonijah to try to seize the kingship, but God alerted David, who ordered that his son Solomon be anointed king, as will appear in this chapter.

1.1.0.en: His servants: those who worked in the royal palace, who were close to the king and cared for his personal affairs. When the attempts of David's servants to warm him did not succeed, they thought of choosing a young virgin to serve him and lie beside him. In this they were imitating what the kings of the surrounding nations did in such circumstances. The young woman would perform this task without being joined to him as a wife, but as a nurse, since King David had become weak, unable to marry, and was suffering from illnesses. This was a Greek remedy that they used to give to the aged in those times, for they thought that a weak body gained energy and vitality when it was joined to a body full of youth and vitality.

1.2.0.en: The Shunammite: from Shunem, a village lying southeast of Nazareth at a distance of seven miles. David's servants searched throughout the whole kingdom for a beautiful young woman for this purpose, and their choice settled on a beautiful virgin named Abishag from the town of Shunem. They brought her to the king, and she was a nurse to him and served him, but David did not have relations with her as a husband does.

1.2.1.en: In the end the body of David, the great man of war, grew weak, and he became unable to carry on with life because of his illness. So do not take pride in your strength or your position, because man is weak by nature and God is the source of strength. Thank Him, use your strength for His glory, and do not be arrogant toward others.

1.3.s.en: (2) Adonijah's attempt to seize the kingship

1.3.0.en: Because of his old age David became unable to carry out his duties as king, so it was necessary to anoint a successor to manage the affairs of the kingdom in the last part of his life. Adonijah the son of Haggith sought to take the throne, since he was the eldest of David's sons then living, and so he considered himself the lawful heir to the throne. Adonijah was David's fourth son, but his firstborn Amnon was killed by Absalom (2 Sam 13), and the second, Chileab (2 Sam 3:3), had died, while the third was Absalom, who was killed when he fought against David (2 Sam 18). Adonijah began to plan to take the kingship and gave his movements a royal appearance: he prepared chariots and horsemen and had fifty men run before him. He was handsome and boasted of his beauty, and David, in his weakness, was unable to rebuke him and prevent him from trying to seize the kingship. Beauty was a desirable thing in kings at that time, but bodily beauty has nothing to do with beauty of spirit and good character.

1.4.0.en: Joab: he was the commander of David's army, and he was harsh and violent.

1.4.1.en: Abiathar: he was a high priest together with Zadok the priest. Abiathar was the one left of the descendants of Eli the priest after Saul killed the priests (1 Sam 22:20). Abiathar was with the ark of the covenant in Jerusalem after he had shared David's afflictions and his flight from Saul. Zadok, for his part, was in Gibeon with the remaining parts of the tabernacle of meeting in the days of David. That is, there were two high priests at the same time in the days of David, and after Abiathar was removed, Zadok became the only high priest in the days of Solomon. In this the word of God was fulfilled, that the house of Eli the priest would be brought to an end (1 Sam 3:11-14). Adonijah began to fortify himself by drawing military and religious leaders around him. Joab, the commander of David's army, responded to him, and so did Abiathar the priest, and they joined him in his rebellion, seeking personal interests and gains. Perhaps Adonijah had promised them that they would continue as head of the army and of the priesthood. Thus Adonijah was relying on the arm of flesh, disregarding the divine will.

1.4.2.en: Perhaps Joab chose to support Adonijah, contrary to God's promise (1 Chr 22:9), because Adonijah was weaker than Solomon, so that through Adonijah's reign Joab could control the kingdom. As for Abiathar, his opposition to God's promise and his support of Adonijah were permitted by God, so that through this evil which Abiathar did, the priesthood would come to an end in the house of Eli the priest, as God had ordered long before by the mouth of Samuel; for Abiathar was the last of the priestly line of Eli.

1.5.0.en: Shimei: a Benjamite, one of David's mighty men, who is the one mentioned in (ch. 4:18) as Shimei the son of Elah, one of Solomon's twelve officers over all Israel.

1.5.1.en: Rei: he is the same as Ira the Jairite mentioned in (2 Sam 20:26), and he was one of the priests in the days of David.

1.5.2.en: At the same time, Zadok the priest, Benaiah, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David's mighty men who loved him were not at ease with Adonijah's actions in his effort to inherit the throne.

1.6.0.en: The stone of Zoheleth: a stone that the Canaanites held sacred, which was one of the landmarks of an area near "En-rogel."

1.6.1.en: En-rogel: a spring near Jerusalem on the border between Judah and Benjamin, in the Kidron Valley south of Jerusalem.

1.6.2.en: Adonijah wanted to give his taking of power a religious character and appearance by offering peace offerings, as though he had received authority from God Himself with the witness of the high priest Abiathar. In this he was imitating Absalom when he made himself king in place of David (2 Sam 15). Adonijah held his conspiracy outside Jerusalem at the stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited his brothers - except Solomon - and the men of the royal court, except those such as Nathan the prophet and Benaiah. This confirms that he was doing something against his father's wishes.

1.6.3.en: So when sin creeps into a person's heart, it blinds him from seeing the truth; he does not accept the divine will and does not turn to wise counsel, but in arrogance relies on his own wisdom and his own opinion. I wish that you would be humble and take refuge in prayer to God, so that you hear His voice and obey Him, and do not oppose Him for the sake of your personal aims.

1.7.s.en: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

1.7.0.en: Nathan was troubled when he heard that Adonijah had made himself king over the children of Israel after David, because he knew that God had declared to David that Solomon would be his successor. This was when He promised him that his son, who would be called Solomon, would be the one to build a house for God, and not David himself (1 Chr 22:29, 1 Chr 28:5, 6), as appears from (v. 30). So he thought of saving the situation and told Bathsheba what Adonijah had done without the knowledge of King David. Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, whom David married and by whom he had Solomon.

1.8.0.en: After Nathan informed Bathsheba of the conspiracy, he invited her to share with him in carrying out a plan opposed to Adonijah's plan, especially since she and her son were in danger of being killed if Adonijah succeeded and took the government, for it is customary that whoever seizes the kingship kills everyone connected with the former king.

1.9.0.en: The plan Nathan drew up was as follows: Bathsheba would go in to David and remind him of the oath he had previously sworn to her, to make her son Solomon king after him, and would ask him why he had not fulfilled what he had pledged, and would tell him of Adonijah's reign. Nathan made her understand that he would follow her immediately to complete the explanation of the matter to the king, because David might not believe Bathsheba's words, but when Nathan confirmed them he would understand and be convinced.

1.10.0.en: In this condition of weakness and old age David did not leave his chamber, for he was not able to go out. Bathsheba had a special familiarity with King David, so she could go in to him at any time to reassure herself about him and to oversee his nursing and his needs. No one was with David except Abishag the Shunammite.

1.11.0.en: Bathsheba went in to the king and showed her great respect by bowing down to the king, so that the king would understand that she was submissive to him, when she reminded him that he had forgotten his promise to make her son Solomon king after him. David sensed that his wife had something she wanted to say, so he encouraged her to speak, saying to her, "What wouldest thou?" It was the custom that no one would enter to the king while he was meeting with one of his wives or one of his counselors, and so Nathan did not enter with Bathsheba until the king called for him.

1.12.0.en: She reminded him first - as Nathan had instructed her - of the oath he had sworn to her, that her son Solomon would reign after him and sit upon the throne of the kingdom.

1.12.1.en: God's promises to you are very many, and you can enjoy them if you hold fast to them and ask Him to give them to you, for He is merciful and tender toward everyone who feels his need and believes in the power of God.

1.13.0.en: She told him what Adonijah had done in declaring himself king without his father's knowledge. She also told him of the feast he had held for this occasion, the sacrifices he had offered in great numbers, and how he had invited to this banquet all his brothers, the king's sons, as well as Abiathar the priest and Joab the commander of the army, but had not invited his brother Solomon.

1.14.0.en: She also pointed to his responsibility toward all his people, who were waiting, with their eyes upon him, for him to declare to them who would sit on the throne of the kingdom after him, for it is not necessary that the firstborn reign after his father, but whomever the king chooses.

1.15.0.en: She made clear to him that after his departure from this world, if Solomon were not declared king, she and her son would be put to death at the hand of Adonijah.

1.16.s.en: (4) Nathan the prophet tells David of Adonijah's conspiracy

1.16.0.en: According to the plan Nathan had drawn up, while Bathsheba was speaking, he arrived; they told the king, who permitted him to enter, and Nathan bowed down before him. Thus Nathan had the opportunity to confirm Bathsheba's words, so that the king would be moved to take the decision to install Solomon as king. What encouraged Nathan was that in this he was carrying out the word of God which He had spoken to David.

1.17.0.en: Nathan asked David wisely, to alert him to the danger, saying to him, "Hast thou said, Adonijah shall reign?!" For he had declared himself king and held a feast, at which the king's sons, the captains of the army, and Abiathar were now gathered. This was to warn the king that a great matter was taking place without his knowledge, and this was contrary to the word of God and to the law of the kingdom, since David had not given them permission for it. Their cry, "God save king Adonijah," implicitly meant that David had died, and this was something that could not be accepted.

1.18.0.en: He also showed him that Adonijah had excluded from this invitation Nathan himself, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and Solomon the son of David, so that the king would understand who those were who were loyal to him and whom Adonijah feared and avoided.

1.19.0.en: Nathan repeated his question to David, whether it was he who had ordered Adonijah to be made king, in order to alert him and urge him to take the opposite decision, that is, to make Solomon king instead of Adonijah. It is understood from this that David was accustomed to making known all his orders to Nathan the prophet, because he represented the presence of God with him.

1.19.1.en: It is wise to alert others and to invite them gently to make decisions without blaming them, for speaking with humility and gentleness wins hearts, lets God work in them, and helps in making decisions.

1.20.0.en: Here David realized the seriousness of the situation and sensed with his wisdom that action had to be taken to set matters right. So he immediately called for Bathsheba, who had gone out from the king when Nathan came in to him, and she came in and stood in the presence of the king after Nathan went out.

1.21.0.en: Once again David renews his oath by the living God, who had redeemed him out of all the distresses that had come upon him, that Solomon would be the one to succeed him in inheriting the throne, assuring Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, that he held fast to his former oath and was renewing it this day also. It is understood from this that God promised David that his son Solomon would reign on his throne (1 Chr 28:5, 6), and that at that time David swore to Bathsheba that he would make Solomon king. This oath is not mentioned in the Holy Bible, and here in this verse he renews his oath.

1.21.1.en: David renewed his oath despite the challenge of circumstances; we too must hold fast to our spiritual pledges and obligations, and not allow worldly preoccupations and temporary matters to hinder our spiritual journey, trusting in the Lord's support for us, so that we may triumph over all obstacles.

1.22.0.en: Bathsheba was reassured and bowed down to the king, expressing her thanks for what he had decided concerning her son, that he would inherit the throne, and she prayed that he would live long, so that the king would not understand from her request to make her son king that she wanted his death. In this Bathsheba obtained what she asked for, namely, that her son Solomon be made king and that she and her son be saved from death at the hand of Adonijah, and at the same time Nathan the prophet attained his aim as a prophet, which was to carry out the orders of God, who had promised that Solomon would be made king.

1.23.0.en: The king went on making the decisions necessary to face the situation and set matters right. He asked his servants to call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and they all came and stood before the king. He called these particular men because Zadok is the priest who would anoint the king, Nathan is the prophet who represents the presence of God, and Benaiah is a military commander who leads the army and protects the new king.

1.24.0.en: Gihon: a spring of water in the outskirts of the city of Jerusalem, that is, outside its walls, which the Jebusites dug in the year 2000 BC. David chose a place outside Jerusalem from which to begin the procession of Solomon's enthronement, so that all the people might see him as he passed. It was customary in ancient times to install kings at springs of water, since they symbolize the continuance of the kingship, like the continual flowing of water from the spring.

1.24.1.en: The king gave them his instructions to take with them the royal guard and those close to the king who were loyal to him, and to set his son Solomon on King David's own mule, which meant that he had become the king, and to go down to Gihon, where Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet were to anoint him with the holy oil as king over Israel, and to blow the trumpets, crying, "God save king Solomon." He sent with the high priest, who was responsible for anointing kings, and with Nathan the prophet, a military force under the command of Benaiah to confront the rebels led by the mighty Joab, should he persist in rebellion. Here we see David's love and humility, for he yielded the kingship to his son while he was still alive, since he felt that it was for the good of the kingdom that his son reign in his place to manage the kingdom with strength and firmness, while it was enough for David to live the remainder of his life in the love of God and the praise of Him.

1.24.2.en: Zadok's anointing of Solomon was in fulfillment of God's law concerning the setting up of kings. As for Adonijah, the Holy Bible does not mention that Abiathar the priest anointed him, but only that he was with him and shared in the celebration, for God did not allow him to be anointed because He was not pleased with his enthronement as king.

1.25.0.en: After he is anointed and proclaimed king, you shall bring him in a royal procession, and he shall sit on the throne and be king in my place. This is my charge to everyone, that he shall rule over Judah and Israel.

1.26.0.en: Benaiah declared his agreement and readiness to carry out the word of King David; indeed, he also declared that this was the word of God, which must be carried out.

1.27.0.en: Benaiah prayed that the Lord would support the new king Solomon in the affairs of government as He had done with his father, and increase him in exaltation and loftiness, and magnify his throne so that it would reach ranks higher even than those which King David himself had reached. This is a prayer that does not anger David, because it is well known that no one wishes anyone else to be better than himself except his son, for when his son achieves more success than he, that is a cause of happiness for his father.

1.28.0.en: The Cherethites and the Pelethites: the police and the army.

1.28.1.en: Those who were loyal to David, namely Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah, together with the police and the army, carried out David's instructions to them. They set Solomon on King David's mule and went with him to Gihon, so that the procession would travel a great distance and the greatest number of the people might see it.

1.29.0.en: The horn of oil: they used to make vessels for liquids from the horns of animals, especially oils and perfumes, among them the anointing oil used to anoint kings and priests.

1.29.1.en: Zadok the priest had taken with him the flask of oil from its place in the tent where the ark of the covenant was (2 Sam 6:17), and there at Gihon he anointed Solomon king, and they blew the trumpets, proclaiming life for King Solomon.

1.30.0.en: All the people responded to the shouts of David's supporters and began to express their joy in the new king by playing on pipes - as was the custom on their occasions of joy - and everyone's joy was overflowing, so that the earth almost split from the force of the echo of their voices.

1.31.s.en: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

1.31.0.en: The city: what is meant by it is Jerusalem, regarded as a limited city compared with the great capitals of the lands such as Babylon and Nineveh. The word "city" in its original linguistic sense may mean a fortress or a citadel, and this means that what is meant is the fortress of Jerusalem, that is, the city of Jerusalem.

1.31.1.en: After Adonijah had made himself king and the guests in his house had finished the feast, they heard the sound of the trumpet and the musical instruments coming from far off from Jerusalem. Joab asked why the sound of the trumpet, since it is not blown except at feasts, or in war, or on special occasions such as the installation of kings.

1.32.0.en: Anxiety spread among all the guests, and meanwhile Jonathan the son of Abiathar the high priest, who accompanied Adonijah, came in, and Adonijah received him eagerly, expecting from him good news that would calm the anxiety of those gathered. Adonijah said to him, "for thou art a valiant man, and bringest good tidings," because he had informed David of the frustration of the wicked counsel of Ahithophel, so that he might prepare for the attack coming upon him from Absalom (2 Sam 15:27, 36; 17:17).

1.33.0.en: Jonathan declared to those gathered that he carried disturbing news for them, namely that David was still holding on to his authority as king, since Jonathan called him "our lord." This shows their error in declaring Adonijah king without David's permission. And also that David had made Solomon king, and this increased the danger of their position and their exposure to harm from Solomon the new king.

1.34.0.en: Jonathan related to them the details of the events: that Zadok had anointed Solomon king at Gihon, with Benaiah and Nathan the prophet with him; that they then set him on King David's mule and went with him in a great procession, with the Cherethites and the Pelethites around them; and that they passed through Jerusalem with great joy and loud voices, which is what the guests had heard from afar while they were in their place.

1.35.0.en: Then Solomon arrived with his procession at the royal palace and sat on the throne of the kingdom, and the servants of King David came in to congratulate him on having made Solomon king, and they prayed that Solomon would be a greater king than he. David rejoiced greatly and bowed himself upon his bed and blessed God, who had granted him to see his son reign after him according to God's promise to him.

1.36.0.en: All the guests at Adonijah's feast were greatly afraid that Solomon the new king would strike them down because of their taking part in this treachery of making another person king without the knowledge of King David, and each one fled his own way to hide from sight, for there was no morality among them; rather each one of them was seeking his own interest and benefit, and now each one was looking for how to save himself even if the others died.

1.37.0.en: Adonijah feared exceedingly that Solomon would punish him for his rebellion, so he hastened to the bronze altar in the tabernacle of meeting to lay hold on its horns, to take advantage of the custom prevailing at that time, namely that whoever laid hold of the horns of the altar was not thereby spared from being killed, but only until a just trial was held in which he could defend himself, clearing himself of the charge brought against him.

1.37.1.en: Adonijah's great fear was a sign of his wickedness, because he had intended to do harm to Solomon and all who followed him, especially since Solomon was known to be strong in character.

1.37.2.en: Do not be hasty in your decisions, lest you fall into matters that cannot be remedied. Take care to pray to God before every action, and even to consult your father of confession, especially in great decisions.

1.38.0.en: If he shew himself a worthy man: that is, loyal to Solomon.

1.38.1.en: They brought him down from the altar: because the altar was set on a high place, but it had no steps (Ex 20:26). Solomon was told what Adonijah had done in laying hold of the horns of the altar, asking that Solomon swear to him that he would be safe and not order him to be killed. Solomon declared that if he was in the wrong he would be punished, and if he was a worthy man no evil would befall him. Then Solomon sent men, and they brought Adonijah to him, and he bowed down before him, trembling.

1.38.2.en: Solomon did not want to begin his reign by punishing anyone, so he allowed him to return to his house, and in this he gave him an opportunity for good conduct, and if he erred a second time he would deserve punishment.

1.38.3.en: David's charge to his son Solomon and the removal of the opponents
